title: zokor
tagline: A backend framework for slang.
text: zokor exists for one reason: a service should spend its code on what it does, not on the plumbing every service rewrites — routing, configuration, error shapes, limits. It is opinionated about the things that go wrong when each service invents its own: one error envelope , one place configuration is read , one router . Copy import "http" ; import "zokor" ; gc struct App { db: pg.Pool, errors: zokor.Registry, } fn show_org (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> http.Response { guard let org = find_org (c.state.db, c. param ( "id" )) else { return zokor. respond (c.state.errors, "org.not_found" , c.request_id); } return zokor. ok_json ( encode (org)); } let r = zokor. new_router (app); r.errors = reg; r. get ( "/orgs/:id" , show_org); r. post ( "/orgs" , create_org); Middleware attaches to a group , not to every handler: Copy r. get ( "/health" , health); // public let api = r. group ( "/api/v1" ); api. before (require_token); // everything below is guarded api. get ( "/orgs/:id" , show_org); api. post ( "/orgs" , create_org); let admin = api. group ( "/admin" ); // nests: /api/v1/admin admin. before (require_admin); // and keeps the parent's hooks admin. delete ( "/orgs/:id" , drop_org); Middleware applies to routes registered after it, on that group, and each route keeps a copy — so adding a hook later cannot silently change a route that already exists. One route on its own: r.guarded(Method.DELETE, "/orgs/:id", drop, [require_admin]) . A before can also resolve something for the handler, which is the point of doing authentication once at the edge: Copy fn require_token (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> opt [http.Response] { guard let user = lookup (c.state.db, c. bearer ()) else { return some (zokor. respond (c.state.errors, "unauthorized" , c.request_id)); } c. set_local ( "user_id" , user.id); // the handler reads c.local("user_id") return none ; } after hooks run innermost first (the route's, then the router's), and they run even when a before stopped the request — so a logging hook cannot be skipped by a short circuit. Methods are a closed set: r.get , r.post , r.put , r.patch , r.delete , r.head , r.options , r.trace , r.connect , and r.any([zokor.Method.GET, zokor.Method.POST], "/p", h) for several at once. A verb the set does not contain answers 501 , not 404 : the path may well exist. Router[S] is generic over your state. A framework cannot know what your handlers need — a database pool, a config, your services — and before slang had generics the only way to reach them was to pass each as its own parameter. A real control plane ended up with a twelve-parameter dispatch that grew with every new service. Here it is one value you declare, and every handler receives it. What is in it Router[S] , Ctx[S] every HTTP method, :params , *wildcards , before/after middleware, automatic HEAD and OPTIONS , Allow on a 405 Registry , respond* every HTTP failure code, one JSON envelope, field-level validation errors load_config , require_* .env plus profiles, startup environment snapshot, per-variable validation, every problem reported at once parse_form , c.upload multipart/form-data: limits, type and extension allowlists, filenames made safe snake_keys , decode_failed , checker DTOs: wire names, decode errors as field errors, validation Json , parse , jobj JSON you did not declare: walk it, build it, render it upgrade , receive , sio_* WebSocket (RFC 6455) and Socket.IO, as a state machine you feed bytes ok_json , created , … success responses with the headers they should carry files_at , r.files(mount) static files: traversal-safe, ranges, validators, cache headers r.compress(compression()) gzip for clients that accept it, on bodies worth it r.idempotency(store) idempotency keys: a retried POST gets the first answer, in memory or Redis page_of , offset_page , cursor_page pagination: offset or keyset pages, one envelope, Link headers new_jobs , every , handle , enqueue background jobs: cron schedules in a time zone, a retrying in-memory queue preconditions , etag_of , r.etags() conditional requests: 304 Not Modified , 412 on a lost update, ETag and Last-Modified redis_from_config a Redis pool from REDIS_URL , optional by default ServerConfig , listen_and_serve_with idle/header/body/write timeouts, safe defaults, all overridable RateLimiter , rate_limit per-client sliding-window limits: 429 , Retry-After , the registered envelope TokenStore , bearer_subject opaque bearer tokens: crypto-random, issue/lookup/revoke, title: Start here
tagline: zokor new writes a service that compiles and passes its tests as it stands, laid out so a person or an agent changing one feature reads one directory: add route registers the route under the feature's prefix (here POST /orders/:id/cancel), behind the feature's authentication, with a handler that answers 501 until it is written and a test that the route is mounted and authenticated.
text: Starting a service # zokor new writes a service that compiles and passes its tests as it stands, laid out so a person or an agent changing one feature reads one directory: Copy make cli # builds bin/zokor bin/zokor new billing # or: --db pg for Postgres cd billing && slangc get && make test && make run bin/zokor add feature orders # a new slice, wired in (--entity to name its type) bin/zokor add route orders POST /:id/cancel cancel_order add route registers the route under the feature's prefix (here POST /orders/:id/cancel ), behind the feature's authentication, with a handler that answers 501 until it is written and a test that the route is mounted and authenticated. zokor check (run by the project's make check ) holds a service to that layout: imports go server -> service -> domain , only store/ and platform/db import pg , domain and service do no I/O, SQL is never built by concatenating a value, configuration is read only in platform/config , every public use case takes a tenant_id , every server.sl is behind require_tenant (or says // zokor:public ), and every package has tests. It prints file:line: rule: message , or one JSON object per line with --json , and exits 1 on any problem. Copy src/main.sl startup only: config, state, mount, serve src/platform/config/ every setting, read once src/platform/app/ App: the state handlers get as c.state src/platform/auth/ who the caller is (API keys -> tenant) src/platform/db/ the Postgres pool (--db pg) src/<feature>/ domain/ types and rules; pure: no I/O, no zokor service/ use cases, and ports.sl: what they need from storage store/ adapters for those ports; store.sl picks one at startup server/ routes, DTOs, error codes migrations/ NNN_<feature>.sql (--db pg), applied by `zokor migrate` Each folder is a package with its tests beside it, and imports run one way: server -> service -> domain , with store implementing the service's ports and platform/app wiring them together. The example feature is a tenant-scoped notes API (create, get, list) behind X-Api-Key , with fakes in *_test.sl so they never ship. add feature writes the same slice under a new name and inserts it at the // zokor: markers in src/platform/app/app.sl and src/main.sl ; it refuses a name that exists or that the generated code uses, and writes nothing then. The project's own AGENTS.md gives an agent these rules in a few lines. A new project pins zokor at v0.2.0 , which is not tagged yet: until it is, pass --zokor-git and --zokor-tag for the commit you build against. The templates are real files under cmd/zokor/templates/ , embedded by make templates ; tests/scaffold.sh (part of make check ) generates both kinds of project against this checkout and runs their tests. Install # In a new project ( slangc new app writes the name and version lines), add the pin to slang.project . The whole file: Copy name app version 0.1.0 pkg zokor git https: //github.com/dolphlabs/zokor tag v0.2.0 dir zokor v0.2.0 is the next release and is not tagged yet. Until it is, pin tag v0.1.0 dir src : the package lived in src/ before the rename. Then fetch it, and import it as import "zokor"; : Copy slangc get dir zokor points the pin at the package inside the repository, so the repository can hold its examples, docs and tests without shipping them into your build. Requirements # slang's dev branch until its next release: typed Postgres mapping needs the compiler-backed pg.rows_as . zokor also needs generic structs and methods and the dir sub-directory pin. HTTPS ( TLS_CERT_FILE ) needs link.tls_accept and served WebSocket and Socket.IO routes need link.split , both on slang's dev branch until its next release.

title: HTTP APIs
tagline: Three helpers.
text: Authentication # Three helpers. Each answers "who is this?" and leaves the policy to you. There are no closures, so keys live in your state and a short before hook passes them in: Copy gc struct App { jwt: zokor.JwtAuth, keys: zokor.ApiKeys } struct Claims { sub: str , role: str , exp: int } fn require_user (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> opt [http.Response] { let r: result [Claims, http.Response] = zokor. bearer_claims (c, c.state.jwt); guard let claims = r else let deny = err_of (r) { return some (deny); } c. set_local ( "user_id" , claims.sub); return none ; } JWTs , HS256 through dolphlabs/jwt : Configuration. jwt_auth_from(cfg) reads JWT_SECRETS (comma-separated, newest first, 32+ bytes each), JWT_AUDIENCE , JWT_ISSUER and JWT_LEEWAY (seconds of clock skew, default 30). Checks. bearer_claims checks the signature, algorithm and duplicate claims, then exp (required), nbf , and aud and iss when configured. Only then does it decode the payload into your own claims type. Failures. Every failure gets the same 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" . token_problem(token, auth, now) gives the reason for your logs. Signing and rotation. sign_token(claims, auth) signs with the newest secret. A token signed with an older listed secret still verifies, so rotation logs nobody out. Basic auth: basic_credentials(c) returns the user and password, keeping a colon inside the password. basic_matches(creds, user, pass) compares SHA-256 digests in constant time, so neither content nor length leaks through timing. basic_denied(c, realm) asks the browser to log in. API keys: API_KEYS=billing:key1,search:key2 , 24+ bytes each, is read by api_keys_from(cfg) . api_key_client(c, keys) reads X-Api-Key and returns the client's name, so a request can be traced to who sent it. Only SHA-256 digests are kept in memory. Every key is compared, in constant time. Operator injection (MongoDB) # MongoDB reads a key starting with $ as an operator. A login handler that passes the body to a query, with a body like {"user":"ada","password":{"$ne":""}} , matches any password. The guard works like express-mongo-sanitize and is opt-in: Copy r. mongo_sanitize (zokor.SanitizeMode.REJECT); // or zokor.sanitize_from(cfg): MONGO_SANITIZE What it checks. Every key of a JSON body, at any depth and inside arrays, and every query-parameter name, decoded first so %24where is $where . A key starting with $ or containing a . is refused. REJECT answers 400 bad_request naming the key, for example body key 'password.$ne' . No before hook and no handler runs. STRIP removes the offending keys and carries on. What it leaves alone. Values are never touched, so "$5 off" is fine. A body that isn't JSON, or isn't valid JSON, is left for the handler to refuse. Cost. With the guard on, a JSON body is parsed once more. SQL has no equivalent on purpose. A blacklist rejects O'Brien and still misses real attacks. The defence is parameterised queries, which the Postgres helpers use exclusively. Cookies # Copy let theme = c. cookie ( "theme" ); // "" when not sent let ck = zokor. new_cookie ( "theme" , "dark" ); // HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/ ck.max_age = 86400 * 30 ; return zokor. set_cookie (resp, ck) ?? resp; // err names what is wrong Safe defaults. A new cookie is HttpOnly , Secure , SameSite=Lax and Path=/ , with no Domain , so it's host-only. Checked before it's sent. set_cookie refuses: a value with a space, quote, comma, ; , backslash or control byte, which could add attributes of its own a bad name a path or domain carrying ; SameSite=None without Secure , which browsers drop a __Host- or __Secure- cookie that breaks its prefix's rules more than 4,096 bytes Reading. c.cookie(name) and c.cookies() skip malformed pairs the way browsers do, and the first of two same-named cookies wins. Deleting. clear_cookie(resp, name, path, domain) removes a cookie ( Max-Age=0 , and an Expires in 1970 for clients that read only that). Lifetime. max_age (seconds; -1 , the default, is a session cookie) is what every browser uses. Set expires too, an instant from timez , for HTTP clients that only read Expires ; when both are sent Max-Age wins: Copy ck.max_age = 3600 ; ck.expires = some (timez. now (). add (timez.HOUR)); // Expires=<HTTP date> Signed cookies carry an HMAC-SHA256 over their name and value, so a client can read them but not change them, or move one to another name: Copy let keys = zokor. cookie_keys_from (cfg); // COOKIE_KEYS=newest,older let ck = zokor. signed_cookie ( "uid" , "42" , keys) ?? zokor. new_cookie ( "uid" , "" ); let uid = zokor. signed_value (c, "uid" , keys) ?? "" ; // none when forged The first key signs and every listed key verifies. To rotate, put the new key first and keep the old one until the cookies it signed have expired; nobody is logged out. Keys must be at least 32 bytes. Signatures are compared in constant time. Signed is not encrypted: never put a secret in a cookie. Conditional requests # A client that already holds the current version gets 304 Not Modified and no body; a write made against a version that is no longer current gets 412 instead of overwriting someone else's change (RFC 9110 §13): Copy fn get_doc (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> http.Response { let doc = load (c); // has .version, .updated_at let tag = zokor. etag_of ( to_bytes ( to_str (doc.version))); if let stop = zokor. preconditions (c, tag, some (doc.updated_at)) { return stop; // 304, or 412 on a write } let resp = zokor. ok_json (json. encode (doc)); return zokor. with_validators (resp, tag, some (doc.updated_at)); } One call for reads and writes. preconditions evaluates If-Match , If-Unmodified-Since , If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since in the order RFC 9110 §13.2.2 sets. A PUT that sends back the ETag it read in If-Match updates only if nobody changed the resource since: optimistic concurrency, no lock. Pass "" as the tag for a resource that does not exist yet, and If-None-Match: * means "create, never replace". Comparisons as the RFC has them. If-Match compares strongly, so a W/ tag never matches; If-None-Match compares weakly. Tag lists, * , and all three HTTP date forms are read; a date that is not a valid HTTP date is ignored, and a malformed tag never matches. r.etags() , opt in: every 200 answer to a GET or HEAD gets an ETag hashed from its body, and a matching If-None-Match gets a 304 that keeps the other headers ( Cache-Control , Vary , …). A response with its own ETag is left alone. It hashes every such body, measured in process ( bench/conditional ): about 1.5 µs a request at 128 bytes, 2.7 µs at 1 KB and 20 µs at 16 KB. With nothing turned on, the request path costs what it did. For a large body, a version you already have ( preconditions ) is far cheaper than hashing the bytes. Security headers # On by default, on every response: dynamic, static, errors, and the 500 after a panic. Copy content-security-policy: default -src ' none '; frame-ancestors ' none ' strict-transport-security: max-age= 31536000 ; includeSubDomains x-content-type-options: nosniff x-frame-options: DENY referrer-policy: no-referrer CSP. An API answers JSON, so its CSP allows nothing: a response opened in a browser runs no script and can't be framed. HSTS. Browsers ignore HSTS on plain HTTP, so it's harmless behind a proxy that ends TLS, and right when the proxy doesn't. COOP and CORP are opt-in: same-origin CORP breaks legitimate cross-origin embeds. Handlers win. A handler that sets one of these headers with with_header keeps its own value. Setting Values SECURITY_HEADERS false turns them all off CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY a policy, or off HSTS_MAX_AGE seconds; 0 is off HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS , HSTS_PRELOAD true / false FRAME_OPTIONS DENY , SAMEORIGIN , off REFERRER_POLICY any standard policy, or off CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY , CROSS_ORIGIN_RESOURCE_POLICY the standard values r.security_headers(zokor.security_from(cfg)) applies the settings, and zokor.no_security_headers() turns them off. Bad values are refused with the fix: an unknown frame option or referrer policy, preload without a year and subdomains, or a CSP containing a line break. Static routes are pre-rendered with the headers, so they cost nothing per request there. On a dynamic response, the five lines add about 10 allocations. CORS # Off by default. One call turns it on: Copy r. cors (zokor. cors_from (cfg)); // CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com,https://*.example.org or r.cors(zokor.cors_policy(["https://app.example.com"])) from code. Setting Meaning Default CORS_ORIGINS exact origins, https://*.example.com for subdomains, or * alone none (off) CORS_METHODS allowed methods GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE CORS_HEADERS request headers a page may send Content-Type, Authorization, X-Request-Id CORS_EXPOSE response headers a page may read X-Request-Id CORS_CREDENTIALS allow cookies and Authorization false CORS_MAX_AGE seconds a browser may cache a preflight 600 The router applies it, so it isn't one more before : Preflights. A preflight to a path that exists gets a 204 with the allowed methods and headers before routing. Neither an auth hook nor a route's own OPTIONS handler can turn it away, and browsers send preflights without credentials. Every response. Any answer to an allowed origin carries its headers: the 404, the 422, a before 's 401 and the 500 after a panic. Without that, the page sees a CORS error instead of the real one. Vary: Origin . It's sent whenever the answer depends on the origin, so a shared cache never hands one origin's answer to another. Other origins. An origin that isn't allowed gets no CORS headers, and the browser withholds the response from the page. A policy is checked before use, and every problem names the fix: an origin with a path or trailing slash, which an Origin header never has a missing scheme upper case a wildcard anywhere but a leading *. * together with credentials, which browsers refuse https://*.example.com matches api.example.com and a.b.example.com , but never example.com or evilexample.com . CORS protects users' browsers, not your server: it is no substitute for authentication. Health and readiness # Copy r. health (); // GET /healthz and GET /readyz r. ready_check ( "db" , db_ready); // what /readyz waits on fn db_ready (s: App) -> result [ int , str ] { let q = s.db. query ( "select 1" ); guard let _rows = q else let e = err_of (q) { return err ( to_str (e)); } return ok ( 0 ); } /healthz is liveness: 200 {"status":"ok"} whenever the process is serving, and it never touches a dependency, so a database outage cannot make the orchestrator restart every replica. /readyz runs every check at once and answers 200 {"status":"ok","checks":{"db":"ok"}} , or 503 with "failing" or "timeout" against each check that did not pass. It also answers 503 shutting_down once SIGTERM arrives, so a load balancer stops sending traffic before the drain. Bounded. A probe waits at most 0.9s ( r.ready_timeout(ns) ), inside Kubernetes' default 1s probe timeout. Isolated. A check runs in its own task, so a panic fails that check, not the probe. A check still running from an earlier probe is joined, not started again, so a hung database costs one task, not one per probe. No leaks. The body names checks, never errors: a driver's message carries hosts and user names. The reason goes to the server's log as a WARN [Health] line, once each time a check starts failing, changes reason or recovers. Out of the way. The router answers these paths only when no route claims them, so your own /healthz wins. No before runs on them, since an auth hook would fail the probes. r.health_at(live, ready) mounts them elsewhere. Static files # Copy let mr = zokor. files_at ( "/assets" , "./public" ); // err if not a directory guard let assets = mr else let e = err_of (mr) { println (e); exit ( 1 ); } assets.max_age = 31536000 ; // hashed names: a year assets.immutable = true ; r. files (assets); A GET or HEAD under the prefix that no route claims is a file from the directory: Traversal-safe. An encoded separator ( %2f , %5c ), a .. , . or dot-file segment ( .env , .git ), a backslash or a NUL is a 404, and the file's real path, every symlink resolved, must be inside the directory's real path or it is a 404 too: a link cannot lead out. Index files. A directory answers index.html ( mount.index ). Validators. ETag from size and modification time, Last-Modified, and 304 / 412 through preconditions . Ranges. One Range: bytes= range is a 206 with Content-Range ( If-Range honoured); one past the end a 416 ; several ranges get the whole file, as RFC 9110 allows. Headers. Content-Type by extension (unknown types are application/octet-stream , which nosniff keeps from being rendered), Cache-Control from max_age ( no-cache by default: revalidate every time, cheap with the validators) and Accept-Ranges . Files are read into memory, up to max_size (64 MB), and the read blocks a worker: serve an app's own assets this way, and put a CDN in front of large or busy ones. Content negotiation and redirects # Compile the representations a handler can serve at startup: Copy let made = zokor. new_negotiator ([ "application/json" , "text/html" ], zokor. accept_limits ()); guard let formats = made else let e = err_of (made) { println (e); exit ( 1 ); } // Keep formats in the router's state. In the handler: let picked = zokor. negotiate (c, c.state.formats); guard let media = picked else let bad = err_of (picked) { return bad; } // Render the selected representation, then return it with media as Content-Type. negotiate combines repeated Accept lines, preserving quoted parameters. It honors q weights, wildcards and parameter specificity: a specific q=0 excludes that representation even when a wildcard permits others. Equal preferences use specificity, client range order, then startup offer order. An absent header selects the first offer; an empty header or no acceptable offer produces the registered not_acceptable 406. Malformed or over-limit headers produce bad_request 400 with an Accept field. All these responses carry Vary: Accept , alongside compression and CORS fields. Negotiator.choose provides selection without a request context. accept_limits() defaults to 8 KB of combined header values, 64 list members, 32 parameters per range (including q), 32 offers and 1 KB per offer. Set these before constructing the negotiator. Configure once and treat its compiled vectors as immutable. Copy let response = zokor. redirect_to ( "/orders/123" ); // checked 303, POST/redirect/GET let rules = zokor. redirect_rules (); // relative references, 8 KB limit rules.allow_external = true ; let moved = zokor. redirect_checked ( 307 , "https://app.example.com/orders" , rules); Checked helpers return a result; they validate 301/302/303/307/308 and preserve the destination with an empty body. Relative paths, queries and fragments are accepted. External HTTP(S) URLs require explicit opt-in; network-path references ( //host ), credentials, raw whitespace, controls, backslashes and malformed percent escapes are refused. Other bytes must be percent-encoded. Errors name the field without echoing the destination. For variable external destinations, the application chooses its permitted hosts. The existing redirect(status, location) remains the raw constructor for destinations the application already controls. Compression # Copy r. compress (zokor. compression ()); // min_size 1 KB, level 1, text-like types A response is gzipped when the client's Accept-Encoding allows it (q values honoured: gzip;q=0 refuses it), it is a 2xx other than 204/206 to a method other than HEAD, its body is at least min_size , its type is text, JSON, JavaScript, XML, SVG or form data (or ends in +json / +xml ), and it has no Content-Encoding of its own. Every response that could have been gzipped carries Vary: Accept-Encoding ; a strong ETag becomes weak. Level 1 is the default: on API JSON it keeps nearly all of level 5's saving (14 KB: 36 µs to 10% of the size, against 74 µs) for half the CPU. Static routes are sent as rendered. BREACH. Over TLS, compressing a response that holds a secret next to input an attacker controls lets them recover the secret from sizes. Keep pages that mix the two (a CSRF token and reflected search terms) on a router without compression. Idempotency keys # A client that retries a POST after a timeout must not charge twice. With Idempotency-Key (the IETF draft), it gets the first answer instead: Copy let store = zokor. idempotency_redis (redis_pool); // or idempotency_in_memory() store.scope_local = "user_id" ; // set by your auth `before` r. idempotency (store); Runs once. A POST or PATCH with the header runs; its answer is kept for 24 hours ( store.ttl ). The same request again gets that answer, with Idempotent-Replayed: true , and the handler does not run. Refuses misuse. The key again while the first is still running: 409 . The key with a different method, path or body: 422 . A key that is not 1–255 printable characters: 400 . store.required = true makes the header mandatory on POST and PATCH. Scoped. Keys are per method, route and caller ( scope_local names the local your authentication sets), so one user cannot replay another's answer. Only final answers. A 5xx, 408 or 429 is not kept: the next retry runs again. Neither is a body over store.max_body (1 MB). A handler that panics leaves its key "running" for store.lock_ttl (30 s). Shared. The Redis store claims a key with SET NX PX , so instances behind a balancer agree; if Redis cannot be reached the request is refused with 503 rather than risk running twice. The in-memory store is for a single instance. Pagination # Offset pages ( ?limit=20&offset=40 ) and keyset pages ( ?limit=20&cursor=… ) answer in the same envelope, so a client reads every list the same way: Copy fn list_orders (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> http.Response { let pr = zokor. page_of (c, 20 , 100 ); // default 20, at most 100 guard let p = pr else let bad = err_of (pr) { return bad; } // 422, named let after = zokor. cursor_parts (p); // [] on the first page // WHERE (created, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT p.fetch() let rows = load_orders (c, after, p. fetch ()); return zokor. cursor_page (c, p, rows, order_key); } fn order_key (o: Order) -> [ str ] { return [o.created, to_str (o.id)]; } Copy {"data":[...],"page":{"limit":20,"cursor":"WyIyMDI2...","next":"WyIyMDI2...","total":null}} One row past the page. p.fetch() is limit + 1 : an extra row means there is a next page, without a COUNT(*) . offset_page takes an optional total when the handler has one. Links. A Link header (RFC 8288) carries rel="next" (and rel="prev" for offset pages), keeping the request's other query parameters. Checked. limit must be 1 to the maximum; offset 0 to 1,000,000 (deeper: use a cursor); not both offset and cursor ; a cursor this API did not issue is refused. Each problem is a named field in a 422. Keyset is the one to use on big tables : the next page is an index range, and rows inserted between requests are neither skipped nor repeated. A cursor is opaque base64url of the last row's sort key; a client can forge one, but only to read another position of a list it may read anyway, so authorise the list, and never put a secret in a key. JSON # slang already does the part Go does badly: you decode into a struct, a missing field is an error rather than a silent zero , and the message names the field. No tags, no interface{} , no omitempty guessing. zokor adds the four things that are still missing. A DTO, decoded and reported. The wire is camelCase, your struct is snake_case, and there are no struct tags — so rewrite the keys: Copy gc struct CreateOrg { name: str , plan: str , seats: i32 , website: opt [ str ] } let r: result [CreateOrg, str ] = json. decode (zokor. snake_keys (c. body_str ())); guard let dto = r else let e = err_of (r) { return zokor. decode_failed (c.state.errors, e, c.request_id); } decode_failed turns slang's own message into the standard envelope with the field named, so a client gets the same shape for a bad type as for a bad value: Copy {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","status":422, "fields":[{"field":"seats","reason":"expected a number, got a string"}]}} {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","status":422, "fields":[{"field":"plan","reason":"is required"}]}} Values, checked all at once. Decoding says a field is a string; it does not say it is an email between 3 and 40 characters. A checker collects every problem, because a client fixing one field per request is a client making five requests: Copy let v = zokor. checker (); let name = v. req_str (body, "name" , 1 , 80 ); let email = v. req_email (body, "email" ); let role = v. req_one_of (body, "role" , [ "admin" , "member" ]); let age = v. opt_int (body, "age" , 0 , 150 , 0 ); if v. failed () { return zokor. respond_fields (c.state.errors, "validation_failed" , v.fields, c.request_id); } req_str , req_int , req_bool , req_email , req_url , req_uuid , req_one_of , req_strs , req_obj , opt_str , opt_int , plus note for a rule of your own and under("address", inner) to report a nested check as address.city . A shape nobody declared — a webhook, a passthrough, somebody else's field. A missing key gives Null rather than an error, so a chain never has to be guarded at every step: Copy guard let body = c. json_body () else { ... } body. get ( "type" ). str_or ( "unknown" ) body. path ( "data.customer.address.city" ). str_or ( "nowhere" ) body. path ( "data.items.0.sku" ). str_or ( "none" ) body. path ( "data.items" ). size () body. has_key ( "note" ) // present, even if null: PATCH semantics Building a response , instead of concatenating strings and getting the quoting wrong: Copy zokor. jobj () . set_str ( "id" , id) . set_int ( "seats" , n) . set_opt_str ( "website" , dto.website) // absent when none . set ( "tags" , zokor. jarr (). add_str ( "a" ). add_str ( "b" )) . render () Numbers keep the text they arrived as, so a 64-bit id survives a round trip; \uXXXX escapes and surrogate pairs decode; and the parser refuses what JSON refuses — a leading zero, a lone surrogate, an unescaped control character, nesting past 64 deep. Uploads # multipart/form-data is a format where being lax is a vulnerability: the client picks the delimiter, names the parts and supplies the filenames. A handler says what it accepts; anything else comes back as a registered failure and never reaches it. Copy fn upload_avatar (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> http.Response { let rules = zokor. with_max_file_bytes ( zokor. uploads_allowing ([ "image/png" , "image/jpeg" ]), 1048576 ); let r = c. upload (rules); // POST/PUT/PATCH only guard let form = r else let e = err_of (r) { return zokor. respond_with (c.state.errors, e.code, e.detail, c.request_id); } guard let avatar = zokor. file (form, "avatar" ) else { return zokor. respond (c.state.errors, "validation_failed" , c.request_id); } zokor. value (form, "title" ); // the non-file fields zokor. files_for (form, "docs" ); // <input multiple> avatar.filename; // safe to use as one path segment avatar.raw_filename; // what the client actually sent return zokor. ok_json ( "{\"bytes\":" + to_str ( len (avatar.data)) + "}" ); } Filenames are made safe : everything before the last / or \ is dropped, control characters go, a leading dot goes, and a name that is empty after that becomes upload . ../../etc/passwd arrives as passwd . The name the client sent is kept as raw_filename for logs. Limits are the caller's , checked while the body is walked: parts, files, bytes per file, bytes per field, total bytes, header size, filename length. Over a size limit is a 413 ; a body that is not well-formed multipart is a 400 ; a type or extension that is not allowed is a 415 . Refused rather than guessed at : a Content-Type that is not multipart or has no boundary, a boundary that is empty or over 70 characters, a body that stops before its closing delimiter, a part with no Content-Disposition or no name, unterminated or oversized part headers, and a Content-Transfer-Encoding the web does not use. A file sent with no Content-Type is refused unless you turn require_content_type off. A body arrives whole, so this does not stream: set max_total_bytes for what a service can afford to hold. Rate limits and bearer tokens # Both are values in your state, shared by every request and safe to use from concurrent handlers (each holds a mutex). Copy gc struct App { errors: zokor.Registry, limiter: zokor.RateLimiter, tokens: zokor.TokenStore, } // 100 requests per client per minute; tokens last a day. Durations // are int nanoseconds, written out: `60 * 1000000000` overflows in // slang today (a product of two literals is computed in 32 bits). let app = App { errors: zokor. new_registry (), limiter: zokor. new_rate_limiter ( 100 , 60000000000 ), tokens: zokor. new_token_store ( 86400000000000 ) }; fn limit (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> opt [http.Response] { return zokor. rate_limit (c, c.state.limiter, c. header ( "x-api-key" )); } fn auth (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> opt [http.Response] { guard let user = zokor. bearer_subject (c, c.state.tokens) else { return some (zokor. respond (c.state.errors, "unauthorized" , c.request_id)); } c. set_local ( "user" , user); return none ; } Refusals. rate_limit answers a refused request with the registered rate_limited code ( 429 , through your renderer if you set one) and Retry-After in whole seconds. Refused requests don't count against the window. Headers on every answer. Allowed or refused, a response carries RateLimit-Limit , RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset (seconds until the next request frees up), so well-behaved clients can pace themselves. Keys. The key is yours to choose: an API key, a user, an address. An empty key shares one "anonymous" budget. rate_limit_client(c, l) keys on the client's address, resolved through TRUSTED_PROXIES , so a client can't escape its limit or spend someone else's by sending a header. Concurrency. The limiter is split into 16 shards, each with its own lock, so tasks checking different clients don't wait on each other. With 8 tasks: 2.0 µs a check, against 17.3 µs with a single lock. Testing. take_at(key, now) and check_at(key, now) take the clock as a parameter, so tests need no sleeps. A before hook that lets a request through can still add headers to its answer with c.add_header(name, value) : the limiter uses it, and so can a hook that refreshes a cookie. TokenStore.issue(subject) returns a 64-hex-character token from crypto.rand ; lookup(token) gives the subject back (expired tokens are dropped), revoke(token) logs one session out and revoke_subject(subject) all of them. Tokens live in memory: they do not survive a restart and are not shared between instances.

title: Data and storage
tagline: slang's pg package is the driver.
text: Postgres # slang's pg package is the driver. zokor adds what every service writes on top of it, and nothing that bypasses it: Copy let pr = zokor. pg_from_config (cfg); // DATABASE_URL, DB_POOL_SIZE (10) guard let db = pr else let e = err_of (pr) { log. error (e); exit ( 1 ); } struct User { id: int , email: str , name: opt [ str ] } fn list_users (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> http.Response { let r: result [[User], str ] = zokor. query_all (c.state.db, "select id, email, name from users where org = $1" , [pg. arg_int (c. param_int ( "org" , 0 ))], until_of (time. mono () + 2000000000 )); guard let users = r else let e = err_of (r) { return zokor. db_failure (c.errors, e, c.request_id); } return zokor. ok_json (json. encode (users)); } Rows into structs, by column name. query_all , query_one (none when there's no row), conn_query_all inside a transaction, and rows_as use slang's compiler-backed pg.rows_as , binding column names once without rendering intermediate JSON text: integers, floats and numerics become numbers (NaN and infinity become strings) booleans stay booleans json / jsonb decode into nested structs NULL becomes none , so use an opt field bytea reads into bytes or a base64 string timestamptz and timestamp become RFC 3339 strings, so a timez.Time field reads them (a timestamp without a zone as UTC), and a str field gets the text an API would send text and uuid become strings A column your struct doesn't name is ignored. A field the query doesn't return must be an opt , or the result names the missing field. Invalid cell storage and type mismatches return errors with row and field context. Transactions. transaction(db, arg, body, deadline) runs body(conn, arg) between BEGIN and COMMIT . An err , a failed COMMIT or a panic in the body rolls back, and the connection goes back to the pool every way out. There are no closures, so what the body needs comes in as arg . Failures in your envelope. db_failure(reg, e, rid) picks the status from the SQLSTATE: unique violation: 409 already_exists foreign key: 409 conflict not null, check, or a bad value: 422 serialization, deadlock or timeout: 503 anything else: 500 The server's message, which names tables, columns and values, never reaches the client. is_unique_violation(e) is there for the common branch. Parameterised queries only. Every helper takes $1 -style SQL and pg.Arg values, and nothing builds SQL from strings. That's the SQL injection defence. Redis # Optional the same way any dependency should be: a service with no REDIS_URL builds no pool and opens no connection. Copy let cfg = zokor. load_config (); let pr = zokor. redis_from_config (cfg); // reads REDIS_URL, REDIS_POOL_SIZE guard let pool = pr else let e = err_of (pr) { println (e); // "REDIS_URL is not set" -- your call whether that's fatal exit ( 1 ); } That is the whole of it: a pool from config, nothing more. Everything past that point is slang's own redis package — redis.acquire , redis.get / set / hset / zadd /…, transactions, pub/sub, streams, cluster routing — called directly, the same way any other zokor service reaches its dependencies. Wrapping the other ~150 functions here would only be a second place for that API to drift from the one slang ships. Copy let cr = redis. acquire (pool, deadline); guard let conn = cr else let e = err_of (cr) { return zokor. respond (c.state.errors, "unavailable" , c.request_id); } let r = redis. get (conn, "session:" + token, deadline); redis. release (pool, conn); Migrations # make cli builds bin/zokor . Run bin/zokor migrate [directory] with DATABASE_URL configured; the default directory is migrations . Files are numbered forward-only SQL, for example 001_create_users.sql . Versions must be positive and unique; descriptions use ASCII letters, digits, underscores or hyphens. Files are ordered numerically. The runner checks every applied filename and SHA-256 checksum, takes a Postgres transaction advisory lock, and applies the whole pending batch in one transaction. A failure rolls back SQL and history together. Keep applied files unchanged and present; add a new file for every change. SQL can contain multiple statements, comments and dollar-quoted function bodies. Explicit transaction/session commands and COPY are refused; nontransactional operations such as CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY belong in a separate operational procedure. Services can call load_migrations(dir, migration_limits()) and migrate(pool, migrations, deadline) at startup. File limits are caller configurable; the CLI reads MIGRATION_MAX_FILES (1000), MIGRATION_MAX_FILE_BYTES (1 MiB), MIGRATION_MAX_TOTAL_BYTES (16 MiB), and MIGRATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (60, maximum 86400). Errors exit nonzero; success prints the applied count, including zero for an unchanged schema.

title: Operations
tagline: Read once, at startup, into a value you hold.
text: Configuration # Read once, at startup, into a value you hold. Nothing reads the environment while serving: a handler that calls getenv changes behaviour without a deploy and cannot be tested without setting process state. Copy let cfg = zokor. load_config (); // .env + .env.<profile>, then environment // or: zokor.load_config_profile("test") // or: zokor.load_config_from("/etc/app/env") // one explicit file let port = zokor. require_port (cfg, "PORT" ); let dsn = zokor. require_dsn (cfg, "DATABASE_URL" ); let from = zokor. require_email (cfg, "ALERT_FROM" ); let mode = zokor. require_one_of (cfg, "MODE" , [ "dev" , "prod" ]); let ready = zokor. check (cfg); guard let _ok = ready else let e = err_of (ready) { println (e); exit ( 1 ); } Profiles are dev , test and prod . load_config() selects ZOKOR_PROFILE from the startup environment or base file, defaulting to dev , and loads .env followed by .env.<profile> if present. The profile file wins over the base file; environment values win over both, including empty values. load_config_profile("test") explicitly selects the test file even if the environment selector says otherwise. cfg.profile is the effective file-selection profile; cfg.sources lists the regular files attempted in precedence order. Values are captured once: changing the process environment after loading does not change get , str_or or the other accessors. For tests and fakes, config_from_values(map) owns a copy of supplied values and reads no environment. load_config_from(path) still loads exactly one file, with no profile overlay, and captures environment overrides once. config_load() supplies options for load_config_with(options) : profile (empty selects the startup selector), directory ( . ), and max_file_bytes (1 MiB per file). load_config_file(path, limit) is the single-file variant with a caller-selected bound. Missing files are optional; directories, NUL bytes, unreadable files and oversized files are errors. All loading and required-value problems reach check(cfg) together. Profile names cannot select arbitrary paths. Every problem comes back together, because a service with six unset variables should say so once instead of failing six times: Copy configuration is not usable (read from .env and the environment): SERVICE_NAME is required but not set PORT must be a TCP port ( 1 - 65535 ), got ' 0 ' DATABASE_URL is required but not set ALERT_FROM must be an email address, got 'ops@' MODE must be one of: dev, prod, got 'staging' Values under a name that looks like a secret ( *_TOKEN , *_PASSWORD , *_URL , *_KEY , …) are reported as (24 characters, hidden) , because this text gets logged. Validators: require , require_int , require_range , require_port , require_bool , require_float , require_email , require_url , require_dsn , require_host , require_ipv4 , require_uuid , require_one_of , require_duration , require_min_len , require_max_len , and optional_url / optional_one_of / optional_dsn for values that must be valid when set . Server timeouts, limits, and shutdown # Safe defaults, not infinite ones: listen_and_serve uses them without asking, and listen_and_serve_with takes a ServerConfig to change any of them. Copy let sc = zokor. server_config_from (cfg); // IDLE_TIMEOUT, READ_HEADER_TIMEOUT, READ_BODY_TIMEOUT, WRITE_TIMEOUT, // MAX_REQUEST_BYTES, MAX_REQUESTS_PER_CONN, SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT, REQUEST_IDS, // TRUSTED_PROXIES, PROXY_HEADER, LOG_FORMAT, LOG_LEVEL, LOG_REQUESTS, // MAX_CONNECTIONS, TLS_CERT_FILE, TLS_KEY_FILE, TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE, // TLS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT spawn zokor. listen_and_serve_with (r, port, sc); Every dynamic request is answered under a request id : the client's own X-Request-Id when it is 1-64 characters of [A-Za-z0-9._-] (so a proxy's id threads through your logs), a fresh req_<32 hex> otherwise. It comes back as X-Request-Id and in every error envelope, the 500 after a panicking handler included, and handlers read it as c.request_id . Static routes are fixed bytes and carry none. REQUEST_IDS=false (or request_ids: false ) turns it off. c.client_ip is who the request came from . By default that is the socket's peer, whatever headers the client sent. Behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, list it in TRUSTED_PROXIES (comma-separated IPv4 addresses and CIDRs, e.g. 10.0.0.0/8,192.168.1.10 ): zokor then reads the proxy's X-Forwarded-For from the right, past every trusted address, and takes the first one that is not -- so a hop the client wrote itself never wins. PROXY_HEADER=forwarded reads RFC 7239 Forwarded instead; only one header is ever believed, so a client cannot add the one your proxy does not set. A bad entry ( 10.0.0.1/8 has host bits set: did you mean 10.0.0.0/8 ?) is reported by check(cfg) with every other problem. Four separate timeouts, not one, because "how long should this wait" has different honest answers depending on what a connection is doing: idle_timeout (default 60s) governs waiting for a request to start on a connection that might legitimately sit open a while; header_timeout (5s) and body_timeout (30s) govern a request that has started arriving and then stalls -- the slow-loris shape a tight window exists to catch; write_timeout (10s) bounds sending the response, separately, since a client that stopped reading is a different problem than one that stopped sending. max_request_bytes (default 16KB) refuses an oversized request at read time -- 431 if the headers alone never complete, 413 if a declared body is bigger than the buffer -- never a silent drop after buffering. max_requests_per_conn (default 100,000) closes a connection after it, answering the request that hit the limit normally first. max_connections (default 10,000, MAX_CONNECTIONS ) caps open connections across every acceptor. A connection past it is answered 503 with Retry-After: 1 and closed at once, so a load balancer retries elsewhere instead of waiting in the accept backlog. Refusals are logged at most once a second. Raise the process's open-file limit ( ulimit -n ) above the cap. If accept fails anyway (out of file descriptors), the loop logs it once and backs off from 5ms up to 1s instead of spinning. Measured on Linux at the limit: a full core spinning before, about 2% after. On SIGTERM / SIGINT , listen_and_serve stops accepting immediately and gives in-flight connections up to shutdown_timeout (default 30s) to finish on their own before returning anyway -- long enough for ordinary requests to complete, bounded so one stuck connection cannot hang a deployment's rollout forever. A panicking handler answers 500 instead of dropping the connection or taking the process down -- the handler call runs isolated in its own task, and the connection closes right after answering rather than serving more requests on whatever state the panic left behind. The static fast path ( GET / , no handler call) never pays for this isolation, since nothing there can panic in the first place. HTTPS # zokor terminates TLS itself when it is given a certificate, so a service can serve HTTPS without a proxy in front of it: Copy TLS_CERT_FILE=/etc/certs/api.pem # the chain, leaf first, PEM TLS_KEY_FILE=/etc/certs/api-key.pem TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE=/etc/certs/ca.pem # optional: mutual TLS TLS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT= 10s # optional, the default server_config_from(cfg) reads them into sc.tls (or set sc.tls = zokor.tls_files(cert, key) by hand), and listen_and_serve_with loads the pair once, before it binds: a missing file or a key that does not match its certificate stops the server starting, with the setting named, rather than leaving it listening on a port where every handshake fails. One file without the other is reported by check(cfg) . Each connection's handshake runs in that connection's own task, under TLS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT , so a client that connects and never speaks holds one connection slot until then and holds up nobody else. A failed handshake -- a port scanner, a plaintext request, a browser dropping a preconnect -- has no request to answer, so it is closed and logged at debug . Past MAX_CONNECTIONS a TLS connection is closed without the plaintext 503, which a TLS client could not read. With TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE , a client must present a certificate signed by one of those CAs. Everything else -- routing, timeouts, keep-alive, WebSockets, logging -- is the same over HTTPS: the serve loop reads and writes the connection as it does plain TCP. A new certificate takes effect on restart. Behind a proxy or load balancer that terminates TLS for you, leave these unset and list it in TRUSTED_PROXIES . Logging # On by default. Every request gets one record, and the server writes its own lines too: routes mapped, listening, shutting down, stopped. On a terminal they look like NestJS's, in colour: Copy [zokor] 51734 - 2026 - 10 - 12 18 : 47 : 01.123Z LOG [Router] Mapped {/users/:id, GET} route [zokor] 51734 - 2026 - 10 - 12 18 : 47 : 01.124Z LOG [Server] Listening on : 8080 + 1ms [zokor] 51734 - 2026 - 10 - 12 18 : 47 : 03.551Z LOG [HTTP] GET /users/:id 200 28B 10.0.0.4 req_1a2b… + 0.41ms [zokor] 51734 - 2026 - 10 - 12 18 : 47 : 04.002Z WARN [HTTP] GET /nope 404 124B 10.0.0.4 req_9f3c… + 0.16ms Anywhere else, such as a pipe, a file or a container's stdout, each line is one JSON object, which is what a log shipper wants: Copy { "time" : "2026-10-12T18:47:03.551Z" , "level" : "log" , "pid" : 51734 , "context" : "HTTP" , "msg" : "GET /users/:id 200 28B 10.0.0.4 req_1a2b…" , "method" : "GET" , "route" : "/users/:id" , "status" : 200 , "duration_ms" : 0.412 , "bytes" : 28 , "request_id" : "req_1a2b…" , "client_ip" : "10.0.0.4" } Setting Values Default LOG_FORMAT pretty , json pretty on a terminal, json otherwise LOG_LEVEL debug , log , warn , error , off log LOG_REQUESTS true , false true NO_COLOR any value colour on a terminal Settings are read by server_config_from(cfg) ; plain listen_and_serve uses the defaults. A 4xx is a warn record and a 5xx an error , so LOG_LEVEL=warn keeps exactly the requests that went wrong. A panicking handler adds an error line with the panic and the request id. What is never logged: query strings, bodies or headers. A matched request is logged by its route pattern, not its path, so ids in paths stay out of the log and a dashboard sees one series per route. An unmatched path is cut to 64 bytes, and control characters, " and \ are percent-encoded, so a client cannot forge a line or send a terminal escape. It never slows a request down. The serve loop hands each record to a bounded queue and moves on, and one task formats and writes the records in batches. If the queue is ever full, records are dropped and counted, and a WARN [Logger] N log records dropped line says so. What it costs. About 3 extra allocations per request. At saturation, GET /users/:id on a laptop with 32 connections went from about 62k to about 50k requests per second, with p99 rising from 1.6–3.0ms to 1.9–3.3ms on the runs not hit by thermal throttling. That's 50k JSON lines a second written to a file. LOG_REQUESTS=false removes the cost and keeps the server's own lines. Bring your own. A Logger is a channel plus a level. To ship records somewhere else, make one with channel_logger(ch, level, requests) , put it in ServerConfig.logger , and drain ch from your own task. new_log_format(pid) gives you zokor's json and pretty formats to reuse. no_logger() turns logging off. Background jobs # Work on a schedule, and work queued to run later, on slang's tasks: Copy let jobs = zokor. new_jobs (state); jobs.logger = sc.logger; jobs.zone = timez. load_zone ( "Europe/Berlin" ) ?? timez. utc_zone (); jobs. every ( "digest" , "0 9 * * MON-FRI" , send_digest, 60 * timez.SECOND); jobs. handle ( "welcome_email" , send_welcome, 5 ); // up to 5 attempts jobs. start (); // ... in a handler: jobs. enqueue ( "welcome_email" , to_str (user.id), timez. now ()); A job is fn(JobCtx[S]) -> result[int, str] ; the context carries the state, the job's name, a queued job's payload and attempt, when the run was due, and a deadline to pass to every call that can block. Schedules in a time zone. Five-field cron (names, ranges, steps, @daily and friends) read on the zone's clocks, so 09:00 in Berlin stays 09:00 across daylight-saving changes (slang's timez ). One run at a time per job. A scheduled job due while its last run is still going skips that turn, with a warning. Missed turns are not replayed after downtime, as in cron. Isolated runs. Each run is its own task: a panic fails that run, logged with the job's name, and the scheduler carries on. Retries. A queued job that returns err or panics is retried after 1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... (capped at an hour) until its attempts run out, then logged and dropped. Shutdown. On SIGTERM the scheduler stops starting runs within a quarter second; runs in progress get the server's shutdown drain. In memory. Queued jobs are lost when the process stops. Work that must survive a restart belongs in a table or a Redis list that a scheduled job drains. Tests set jobs.clock = timez.fixed_clock(...) and call jobs.tick(instant) and jobs.wait_runs(timeout) : no sleeping. Errors # Every failure names a code; every code is registered once with its status and its wording; every response is rendered by the same function. A client sees one shape: Copy {"error":{"code":"org.not_found","message":"no such organisation", "status":404,"request_id":"req-9"}} Copy {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"some fields are not valid", "status":422, "fields":[{"field":"email","reason":"must be an email address"}]}} All HTTP failure statuses ship registered ( bad_request … network_auth_required ). Add your own, or reword a built-in: Copy zokor. register (reg, "org.not_found" , 404 , "no such organisation" ); zokor. register (reg, "rate_limited" , 429 , "slow down" ); A code nobody registered answers 500 and names itself — the mistake belongs in your logs, not hidden behind a generic message. The shape is a default # That envelope is what you get until you say otherwise. A service with an existing contract — a different key, application/problem+json , whatever its clients already parse — installs its own renderer and keeps the registry, the codes and the statuses: Copy fn problem_json (v: zokor.ErrorView) -> http.Response { let body = "{\"type\":\"about:blank\",\"title\":" + zokor. quote (v.code) + ",\"detail\":" + zokor. quote (v.message) + ",\"status\":" + to_str (v.status) + "}" ; return zokor. bytes_of (v.status, "application/problem+json" , to_bytes (body)); } zokor. set_renderer (reg, problem_json); ErrorView carries the code, the message, the status, the request id and the field errors — a struct, not a parameter list, so a later addition does not break renderers people have already written. One renderer per registry: every failure in a service still comes out the same way, which is the point of having a registry at all. Metrics # Metrics are opt-in: build new_metrics(metrics_config()) , check its result, then call r.metrics(metrics) . The default endpoint is GET /metrics (HEAD also works), in Prometheus text format 0.0.4. It answers on a routing miss, so an explicit service route wins; the built-in scrape skips before hooks and does not count itself. zokor_http_requests_total and zokor_http_request_duration_seconds (cumulative histogram buckets, sum and count) label by method, registered route pattern and status. Client ids and unmatched paths never become labels: misses use __unmatched__ , unknown methods use OTHER . zokor_http_in_flight covers dispatch and response writing, including static responses; panics complete as 500. Idle connections are excluded. MetricsConfig chooses the path, max_series (1000), max_custom (100), and increasing buckets_ns ; exposition uses seconds. Configuration errors name every bad field. Beyond the series cap, completions increment zokor_http_observations_dropped_total ; in-flight accounting still ends. Counters saturate at the largest integer rather than wrapping. Register service signals with metrics.counter("jobs_completed_total", "Completed jobs") or metrics.gauge("queue_depth", "Queued jobs") ; each returns a checked Metric . add(delta) rejects negative counter deltas and overflow; set(value) is for gauges. Names use Prometheus ASCII identifiers, with zokor_ reserved. Registration, updates and scrapes are concurrency-safe, and the framework reads no environment while serving. Tracing # Tracing is opt-in: check new_tracer(trace_config()) , then call r.tracing(tracer) at startup. c.trace() returns the request's TraceContext (trace id, incoming parent id, current span id, sampled bit and vendor state). Missing, invalid or duplicate traceparent headers start a fresh trace; malformed tracestate is dropped without changing a valid parent. Limits default to 256 parent bytes, 512 state bytes and 32 state members, and can be lowered in TraceConfig . Use c.trace_request(request) before an httpc call. Check its result; it returns a copy with lowercase W3C headers and a fresh child span, without changing the original request or headers. For background work, pass c.trace() explicitly and call trace_request(context, request) . No context lives in thread-local storage. c.logger(logger) binds application log lines to the trace and request id; traced_logger(logger, context) does the same for an explicit context. Server request records and panic lines carry the same trace id. JSON logs always include trace_id (empty outside a trace); pretty logs append it when present. Framework errors use the request's c.errors registry: the default envelope includes error.trace_id when traced, and custom renderers receive it in ErrorView.trace_id . The startup registry remains shared and is never mutated per request. Use trace_registry(registry, context) for errors outside a handler. Sampling is propagated as a flag; this feature supplies context and correlation, without exporting spans. Entropy failures return an error from propagation helpers and a registered 500 from request dispatch. Tracing off creates no per-request context, registry or locals map. Idempotent replays retain the original response body, including its original error trace id; the replay's request log records the new trace. OpenAPI # Build an OpenAPI 3.1.1 document at startup from r.routes_list() and explicit JSON wire schemas. The generator reads no environment, creates no endpoint, and does no reflection over slang types. Copy let api = zokor. new_openapi ( "Users API" , "1.0.0" ); api. schema ( "User" , "{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"id\":{\"type\":\"integer\"}},\"required\":[\"id\"]}" ); let op = zokor. api_operation (zokor.Method.GET, "/users/:id" ); op.operation_id = "getUser" ; push (op.parameters, zokor. api_parameter ( "id" , "path" , "integer" )); push (op.responses, zokor. api_response ( 200 , "User" )); push (op.errors, "not_found" ); api. operation (op); let generated = zokor. openapi_document (r. routes_list (), r.errors, api); // Check generated before saving or serving its JSON text. ApiOperation declares an optional request_schema , request media type and required flag, response status/media/schema pairs, parameters, tags, summary and description. Schema names refer to registered DTOs; string , integer , number , boolean , object , array and null are inline primitives. api_ref(name) builds a reference definition. Schemas may use local component JSON pointers and recursive references; the generator preserves composition, formats and examples. It checks schema structure and references; services should also validate the full JSON Schema dialect in their contract checks. :id becomes {id} with a required string path parameter unless its metadata supplies another type. Routes without response metadata get a default response labelled as undeclared; success status and shape are never inferred. Exact duplicate registrations use the first route, matching the router. Colliding templates, duplicate operations or ids, unregistered metadata, invalid parameters, unknown schemas and unknown error codes are reported together. Unsupported CONNECT or wildcard routes must be explicitly excluded with api.omit(method, pattern) . Use the same method to exclude private routes from a published document. The document includes registered error codes, statuses and messages in x-zokor-error-codes ; an operation's errors adds responses grouped by status. Error body contracts are explicit. For the default renderer, register api_default_error_schema() under your chosen name and set api.error_schema to that name. A custom renderer supplies its own schema and api.error_media_type . Without one, error responses make no body claim. Authentication metadata is not inferred from hooks; services can extend the generated JSON with their security schemes and requirements. api.limits defaults to 1000 routes, schemas and entries per metadata collection, 1 MiB per schema, 16 MiB total schema text and metadata text, schema depth 32 (maximum 64), and 16 MiB of generated JSON. Limits are caller-selected. Output preserves route registration order and sorts schema/error names, so map insertion order does not change it.

title: Realtime connections
tagline: A WebSocket route is a handshake handler plus the handlers for what happens after it.
text: WebSocket # A WebSocket route is a handshake handler plus the handlers for what happens after it. The handshake goes through the router like any request -- its before s run, so authentication, rate limits and CORS apply -- and once the 101 is written the connection belongs to the socket: Copy fn chat_open (c: zokor.Ctx[App]) -> http.Response { if c. local ( "user" ) == "" { // set by an auth before return zokor. respond (c.errors, "unauthorized" , c.request_id); } let s = c. socket (); // not yet open s. set_local ( "user" , c. local ( "user" )); c.state.hub. join_room (s, "lobby" ); return c. accept_ws (); // the 101; anything else refuses } fn chat_message (app: App, s: zokor.Socket, m: zokor.Message) { app.hub. to_room ( "lobby" , s. local ( "user" ) + ": " + m.text, s.id); } fn chat_left (app: App, s: zokor.Socket, code: int , reason: str ) { ... } r. websocket ( "/chat" , chat_open, zokor. ws_route (zokor. ws_allowing ([ "chat" ]), chat_message) . on_close (chat_left)); s.send_text , s.send_binary and s.close(code, reason) work from any task -- this socket's handler, another connection's, a background job -- and never wait: a send queues the message, and the connection's writer task puts it on the wire. A Hub holds sockets by id and in rooms: add , join_room , leave_room , broadcast , to_room , get , count , room_size . A socket leaves every hub it was in when its connection ends. The hub is in-process; several instances need their own fan-out between them (Redis pub/sub, say). Each connection is two tasks: one reads, decodes and calls the handlers in order, one message at a time; the other writes. What the settings in WsRules bound, and what happens at each: A client that stops reading fills its queue ( max_queue , 256 messages) and is closed instead of holding memory, or the broadcaster, hostage. A peer that vanished without a FIN is pinged after ping_interval (25s) of silence and closed pong_timeout (20s) later. A handler that panics closes its connection with 1011; every other connection carries on. on_close runs once however the connection ended, with the peer's code, ours, 1002 for a protocol error or 1006 when the peer vanished. SIGTERM closes every open socket with 1001 ("server shutting down"), so clients reconnect elsewhere, before the drain. Over TLS ( TLS_CERT_FILE ) the same route serves wss:// . Underneath, a connection is a state machine, not a socket ( new_conn , receive , pending ): bytes in, whole messages and bytes to send out. That is what the tests drive without a network, and what refuses, with 1002, an unmasked client frame, a reserved bit or opcode, a fragmented or oversized control frame, a length that is not minimally encoded, a continuation with nothing to continue, a new message before the last finished, text that is not UTF-8, an invalid close code, and anything over max_frame_bytes / max_message_bytes . Ping/pong and the closing handshake are answered by the connection, because they are protocol rather than application. Socket.IO # socket.io clients (socket.io-client 3 and 4: Engine.IO v4, Socket.IO v5) on the same server, with the same handshake handler shape: Copy fn on_chat (app: App, s: zokor.Socket, e: zokor.SioEvent) { if e.name == "chat message" { app.hub. emit_to_room ( "lobby" , e.namespace, "chat message" , e.args_json, s.id); if e.ack >= 0 { s. ack (e.namespace, e.ack, "[\"delivered\"]" ); // the client's callback } } } r. socketio ( "/socket.io/" , chat_open, zokor. sio_route (on_chat). on_connect (joined). on_disconnect (left)); on_connect(app, s, namespace, auth_json) accepts a namespace with ok(true) or refuses it with err(message) , which the client sees as a connect_error ; without one every namespace is accepted. Events for a namespace the client is not connected to are dropped. s.emit , s.emit_with_ack (the answer arrives as an Ack event), s.ack and s.disconnect_ns send; hub.emit_all and hub.emit_to_room encode an event once for every Socket.IO session they reach. A hub can hold WebSockets and Socket.IO sessions together: to_room reaches the first, emit_to_room the second, so a chat open to both calls both. on_disconnect(app, s, namespace, reason) runs once per connected namespace with socket.io's reasons ( client namespace disconnect , transport close , ping timeout , server shutting down , server error for a panicking handler). The Engine.IO heartbeat is run for you on route.settings ( ping_interval_ms , ping_timeout_ms , max_payload ). Both of socket.io's transports are served, so a client needs no options: it starts on HTTP long-polling (a GET that waits for packets, a POST that carries its own) and moves to WebSocket once a probe over it succeeds, or stays on polling where WebSockets do not get through. The session -- its id, hubs, namespaces and locals -- is the same Socket throughout, and handlers cannot tell which transport a packet came by. Polling sessions live between requests: they are capped by max_polling_sessions (10,000; past it the handshake is answered 503), and one heartbeat task per route pings them and ends those that stop answering. Two GETs or two POSTs at once for one session end it, as Engine.IO requires. A polling POST is one HTTP request, so it is bounded by MAX_REQUEST_BYTES (16KB by default): raise it towards max_payload if clients send large events over polling. Binary attachments work both ways. An event's attachments arrive in e.attachments (in order; args_json holds a placeholder where each was), and s.emit_binary(namespace, name, args_json, [data]) / hub.emit_binary_to_room(..) send them: binary frames over WebSocket, base64 over polling. An event may carry up to max_attachments (16). examples/chat is one room for both kinds of client, served for real: make example-chat runs it against stand-in clients, and slangc examples/chat/main.sl --run -- serve serves it on :8080 for a browser. Checked against socket.io-client 4.7.5 and the ws package.

title: Project structure
tagline: A request builder and response readers, so a test says what it means instead of assembling an http.Request by hand: request, get request, .header, .bearer, .basic, .content type, .json, .json body, .body str, .multipart (with upload part), and on the way back resp status, resp text, resp header, resp json, resp error code, resp error fields.
text: Testing # A request builder and response readers, so a test says what it means instead of assembling an http.Request by hand: Copy let resp = r. serve (zokor. request (zokor.Method.POST, "/api/orgs" ) . bearer ( "token" ) . json_body ( "{\"name\":\"acme\"}" ) . build ()); assert (zokor. resp_status (resp) == 201 ); assert (zokor. resp_json (resp). get ( "id" ). str_or ( "" ) == "org_7" ); assert (zokor. resp_error_code (denied) == "unauthorized" ); assert (zokor. resp_error_fields (invalid)[ 0 ] == "seats" ); request , get_request , .header , .bearer , .basic , .content_type , .json , .json_body , .body_str , .multipart (with upload_part ), and on the way back resp_status , resp_text , resp_header , resp_json , resp_error_code , resp_error_fields . It ships in the package because your service's tests need it too. Layout # Copy zokor/ the package your service imports router.sl Router[S], Route[S], Ctx[S] errors.sl Registry, Code, ErrorView, the envelope config.sl Config, load_config, require_* respond.sl success responses ids.sl request and session ids json.sl Json, the checker, DTO helpers testkit.sl the request builder and response readers upload.sl uploads: rules, Form, Upload, safe filenames ratelimit.sl RateLimiter, rate_limit tokens.sl TokenStore, bearer_subject ws.sl WebSocket connections and Socket.IO socket.sl Socket, Hub: a served connection and its rooms ws_serve.sl r.websocket: the handshake and a connection's two tasks sio_serve.sl r.socketio: Engine.IO sessions over the WebSocket internal/ path/ split, query parsing, percent-decoding envfile/ .env parsing validate/ the value rules multipart/ the multipart/form-data parser ws/ RFC 6455 frames and the handshake sio/ Engine.IO and Socket.IO packets examples/ hello/ routes, config, errors, DTOs, uploads chat/ WebSocket and socket.io www/ docs-site builder, theme and resized logo assets assets/ the logo todo.md what is next, checkable docs/ generated site, benchmarks, llms-small.txt (the agent guide: every snippet compile-checked by `make snippets`), api.txt (every public symbol, generated by gen_api.sh) .github/ CI: tests, guide snippets, API and site freshness internal/ holds the pure parts: no sockets, no clock, no environment. That is where the tests are cheapest and the hot paths easiest to keep honest. Tests # Copy make test make check runs the tests, all examples, the agent guide's snippets ( docs/llms-small.txt , via make snippets ), and the API and site freshness checks. CI runs the same against slangc built from slang dev . Dependencies: ports and fakes # Use a struct of function values, wired once at startup. A service holds that port and calls it; concrete database or HTTP clients live in adapters. Slang has no closures, so pass adapter state explicitly rather than hiding it in globals: Copy pub gc struct StockPort[C] { context: C, lookup: fn (C, str , str ) -> result [ opt [Stock], str ], } // A top-level adapter function has the same signature: // lookup(context, tenant_id, sku). Startup injects its function and context. The application defines the port. Infrastructure imports that definition and implements it; application code imports domain types and never the adapter. The bootstrap imports both and connects them. Tenant identity remains an explicit argument through each call. An optional result separates a missing record from an unavailable dependency. The HTTP edge maps failures to registered errors without exposing adapter diagnostics. examples/ports/src/main.sl is the worked example: a tenant-scoped stock service, an immutable memory adapter, a protected route, and startup configuration. make example-ports drives the real router pipeline without opening sockets. It prints an unauthenticated 401, the seeded stock, and a registered missing-stock 404. The existing hello/chat examples keep their behavior. Application fakes live in fakes_test.sl , so the compiler excludes them from service builds. They supply the same function signature with their own explicit state, return canned success/absence/failure, and record calls. Tests prove that invalid input never reaches a port, tenant identity is passed through, another tenant's record is rejected, unauthenticated HTTP requests cannot invoke the port, and adapter details do not reach clients. make test lists all four example packages; make check also runs its startup wiring. For generic application services, use small concrete top-level route functions in the bootstrap to call the generic HTTP helpers. The example uses this ordinary function-value pattern for registration and gives tests their own wrappers. Each adapter owns its concurrency rules: the example copies its seed data once and never mutates it after startup; a mutable adapter must synchronize its state. Agent guide # An agent writing a service reads slang's llms-small.txt then docs/llms-small.txt : one page, example-first, with the one way for errors, config, validation, routing and tests, and recipes for headers, rate limits, bearer tokens, uploads, shared state, background workers and graceful shutdown. Every snippet in it is a whole program that compiles and runs; make snippets proves it. docs/api.txt is the companion: every public symbol, its signature and one line, small enough to keep in context instead of reading zokor/ . It is generated ( make api , which runs docs/gen_api.sh ); CI fails if it is stale. make docs builds the static site at docs/index.html from this README, the generated API reference and the service examples. make docs-check fails when the committed site is stale. Not yet # The full list, ordered and checkable, is todo.md . The remaining work is the v0.2.0 release after slang ships the required compiler and package features, the measured performance gap described in docs/benchmarks.md , and the MongoDB adapter, which is currently deferred. The HTTP, realtime, migrations, metrics, tracing, pagination and OpenAPI work listed earlier in this README is implemented.
